analysis.one_liner: Makes core PATRIOT Act surveillance powers permanent and gives the FBI new power to demand Americans' records.
analysis.headline: The Senate Intelligence Committee reported the bill on June 16, 2005 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This Senate Intelligence Committee bill would have removed the December 31, 2005 expiration date from the central surveillance powers in the USA PATRIOT Act — including roving wiretaps, access to business records, and pen registers — making them permanent [S2, S3]. It would have given the Attorney General and the FBI a new administrative subpoena power to compel financial, credit, telephone, and internet-provider records without first going to court [S3, S4], and it would have written into law the FBI's practice of 'mail covers,' in which the Postal Service must record mail delivered to a target [S3, S4]. The bill did add some safeguards — recipients of record orders could consult a lawyer and petition a secret court, and the Attorney General would report how often libraries, bookstores, gun dealers, health records, and tax records were targeted [S3]. It never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The FBI and the Justice Department gain the most: their most-used surveillance tools would never expire again, and they would get a new administrative subpoena power to demand financial, credit, telephone, and email-provider records directly, plus legally mandated Postal Service cooperation with mail covers [S3, S4]. Telephone and internet providers, banks, and credit bureaus also gain a liability shield — immunity from being sued by customers for handing over their records in good faith [S4].

how_it_helps.text: It would make permanent, with no more expiration date, the PATRIOT Act's core surveillance tools: information sharing, roving wiretaps, pen registers and trap-and-trace devices, business records access, and FISA electronic surveillance orders [S2, S3].

It would create a new administrative subpoena power letting the Attorney General and FBI designees compel financial, credit, telephone, and internet-provider records in terrorism investigations without first going to a court, enforced by contempt if refused [S3, S4].

It would write national security mail covers into law, requiring the Postal Service to turn over records of mail to and from a target whenever the FBI certifies relevance to a national security investigation [S3, S4].

It would extend, to 2009, the redefinition of 'agent of a foreign power' to include individuals engaged in international terrorism, and lengthen how long pen-register and trap-and-trace orders can run — up to a year for foreign powers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary Americans pay in privacy: their library borrowing, bookstore purchases, gun purchases, health records, tax records, bank and credit records, phone metadata, and even the outside of their mail could all be obtained by the FBI, generally with gag orders preventing them from ever being told [S3, S4]. Businesses and libraries pay in compliance burdens and, if they speak about an order, criminal penalties of up to five years' imprisonment [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill would have removed the December 31, 2005 sunset from the most sweeping PATRIOT Act powers — roving wiretaps, business records access, pen registers and trap-and-trace devices — making them permanent without the periodic re-debate the sunset was designed to force [S2, S3].

The bill would have rewritten FISA's definition of 'contents' so that it no longer covered information about the identity of the parties to a communication, narrowing what counts as protected communication content under the surveillance law [S3].

Supporters would point out that the bill did add checks: a 'relevant to' standard for business records, the right to consult a lawyer and petition the FISA Court, minimization procedures, semiannual reports on library, bookstore, firearm, health, and tax records, and a bar on investigations based solely on First Amendment activity [S3, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was not purely one-sided: it replaced the broad 'sought for' standard with a stricter relevance requirement, gave recipients of business-records orders a lawyer and a court petition, and added reporting on sensitive record categories — real, if modest, checks [S3]. But those gains were traded for the largest thing the bill did: strip the December 31, 2005 sunset from the core surveillance powers, including roving wiretaps, national security letters' record access, and pen registers, and add administrative subpoenas enforceable with contempt [S2, S4]. For anyone weighing the bill as a citizen, the permanence and the new subpoena power outweigh the procedural safeguards bolted on. That the bill never came to a vote meant those tradeoffs were never debated in the open.

outcome.mechanism: The Intelligence Committee reported the bill straight to the Senate floor calendar in June 2005, but no senator ever brought it up for a vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: On June 16, 2005, Senator Pat Roberts reported the bill to the Senate as an original measure from the Select Committee on Intelligence, with written report No. 109-85 and additional and minority views filed [S6].
The same day it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 132 — and the action record shows no further steps: no motion to proceed, no debate, no vote [S6].

The bill would have removed the December 31, 2005 sunset date from the central PATRIOT Act surveillance authorities and added new subpoena and mail-cover powers, so while it sat on the calendar those powers remained scheduled to expire and required new legislation to survive [S2, S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one converted this bill into law, so the December 31, 2005 sunset on the core surveillance powers stayed in place and any continuation had to be negotiated through new legislation — a temporary win for privacy-minded senators and for members of the public who wanted these powers debated in the open rather than made permanent by a single committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Privacy-minded senators; the sunset stayed in force

for.name: Sen. Pat Roberts
for.role: Chair, Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate as an original committee measure on June 16, 2005 and had it placed on the Senate calendar [S6].

against.name: Senate Intelligence Committee minority
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views alongside the committee report, signaling formal disagreement with the bill as reported [S6].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee claiming jurisdiction over PATRIOT Act reauthorization
against.what_they_did: Asserted its own jurisdiction over the PATRIOT Act reauthorization and advanced a competing bill, leaving the Intelligence Committee's version without a clear path to the floor. This rivalry was extensively covered at the time and is not reflected in the action record.

against.name: The Senate
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; it sat on the calendar for the remainder of the 109th Congress with no motion, debate, or vote [S6].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had zero cosponsors and was reported by the Republican chairman of the Intelligence Committee, but no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the partisan split cannot be measured [S5, S6].

industries.note: Providers would be compelled to furnish subscriber records — names, addresses, payment mechanisms including credit card and bank numbers — under pen-register and administrative-subpoena authority, but would receive immunity from civil liability for good-faith production [S4]. Compliance costs go up; legal risk goes down.

industries.industry: Banks, credit bureaus, and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: The bill would direct the FBI to use its new administrative subpoena power to obtain financial institution customer records, financial information, and credit agency consumer records, with gag orders attached [S3, S4]. The industry's interest in not being compelled to hand over customer data runs in the same direction as customers' privacy interest.

The bill keeps FBI access to library and bookstore records and adds semiannual reporting on how often they are targeted — an acknowledgment of how sensitive that access is [S3]. Gag orders would prevent them from telling patrons.
The Postal Service would be legally required to comply with every FBI mail cover request and barred from disclosing that it did so, turning a long-standing informal practice into statute [S4].
